title: Buying and Selling at the Same Time

chapters.title: Introduction
chapters.html:
Selling your current property and buying a new one at the same time is a balancing act: financial, logistical and timing questions all intertwine. Well planned, it's done calmly.

This guide covers the scenarios (sell first, buy first), the tools to bridge the gap, and coordinating the dates.

Each chapter ends with a lined “My notes” page.

Selling your property and buying another at the same time is a balancing act: finances, logistics and timing intertwine. This guide covers choosing the sequence, the tools to bridge the gap, coordinating the dates and how to avoid carrying two properties.

Well planned, the exercise becomes a simple series of controlled steps.

chapters.title: Sell first or buy first?
chapters.objective: Choosing the sequence suited to your risk.
chapters.html:
Choosing the sequence suited to your risk.

Everything comes down to the order of operations, and each has its downside:

  • Sell first: you know your exact budget and sell without pressure, but risk having to find temporary housing.
  • Buy first: you secure your next home, but risk paying for two properties if the old one is slow to sell.

The sale condition (making an offer conditional on the sale of your property) is a tool to reduce this risk.

Everything comes down to the order: sell first (exact budget known, no pressure, but the risk of finding temporary housing) or buy first (next home secured, but the risk of paying for two properties). The sale condition (offering conditional on the sale of your property) reduces this risk.

Emilie's tip

If your budget can't absorb two mortgages, lean toward “sell first” or use a sale condition. Peace of mind is often worth more than the perfect house found too early.

chapters.title: Bridging the financial gap
chapters.objective: Managing the lag between the two transactions.
chapters.html:
Managing the lag between the two transactions.

If the dates don't coincide, or if you buy before receiving your sale proceeds, tools exist:

  • Bridge loan: temporary financing until the sale proceeds come in.
  • Line of credit: to cover a short gap.
  • Negotiating compatible possession dates.

The bridge loan is the most common tool: it covers precisely the gap between the purchase and the sale.

If the dates don't coincide, tools bridge the gap: the bridge loan (temporary financing until the sale proceeds come in), a line of credit, or negotiated possession dates. Talk about the bridge loan with your mortgage broker BEFORE making an offer.

Emilie's tip

Talk about the bridge loan with your mortgage broker BEFORE making an offer. Knowing that the financial bridge is possible (and at what cost) completely changes your room to maneuver.

chapters.title: Coordinating dates and logistics
chapters.objective: Orchestrating the two closings and the move.
chapters.html:
Orchestrating the two closings and the move.

Ideally, align the possession dates (sale and purchase) as much as possible for a smooth move.

Failing that, plan for:

  • Temporary storage.
  • Transitional housing.
  • A margin in the schedule.

A broker who handles both transactions can synchronize the deadlines and anticipate the friction points.

Ideally, align the possession dates for a smooth move; failing that, plan for storage, transitional housing and a margin in the schedule. A broker who handles both transactions can synchronize the deadlines and anticipate the friction.

Emilie's tip

Ideally entrust the purchase AND the sale to the same broker. They see both calendars at once and can line up the dates to save you a double move.

chapters.title: Avoiding costly double holding
chapters.objective: Limiting the risk of paying for two properties.
chapters.html:
Limiting the risk of paying for two properties.

The worst scenario is ending up with two properties on your hands. A few safeguards:

  • Price your current property well so it sells fast.Use a
  • sale condition on the purchase when possible.Negotiate
  • flexible dates on the seller's side.Keep a
  • financial cushion to absorb a few weeks of overlap.Anticipating the worst scenario is exactly what keeps you from living it.

The worst scenario is two properties on your hands. Safeguards: price your current property well so it sells fast, use a sale condition, negotiate flexible dates and keep a cushion. Don't overprice “just in case”: that's what makes sales drag on.

Emilie's tip

A well-priced, well-presented property sells faster — and that's your best protection against double holding. Don't overprice “just in case”: that's what makes sales drag on.

A successful sequence follows an outline: determine the sequence according to my risk, validate the financing and the bridge loan, go to market or shop in parallel, coordinate the dates, then synchronize the two closings. Write your plan on one page with the key dates.

Write your game plan on a single page with the key dates. With the overview in hand, the decisions become obvious and the stress comes down.

chapters.title: Action plan
chapters.html:
Your next steps, concretely.

This week

  1. Determine my sequence (sell or buy first).
  2. Assess my ability to absorb a gap.

Within 30 days

  1. Explore the bridge loan with my mortgage broker.
  2. Coordinate the possession dates.

Next

  1. Entrust both transactions to the same broker to synchronize everything.

My game plan

  1. Determine my sequence and explore the bridge loan before making an offer.
  2. Coordinate the possession dates and keep a safety cushion.

chapters.title: Resources & glossary
chapters.html:
• Sale condition: making an offer conditional on the sale of your property.
  • Bridge loan: temporary financing covering the gap between purchase and sale.
  • Possession date: the date of taking possession, to be coordinated.
  • Double holding: a period when you hold two properties, to be minimized.
  • Sequence: sell first or buy first, according to risk.
  • Sale condition: making an offer conditional on the sale of your property.
  • Bridge loan: temporary financing covering the purchase/sale gap.
  • Possession date: the date of taking possession, to be coordinated.
  • Double holding: a period when you hold two properties, to be minimized.
  • Sequence: sell first or buy first, according to risk.
